abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD), characterized by the accumulation of amyloid {beta}-peptide (A{beta}) plaques, is a progressive age-related neurodegenerative disorder affecting more than 35 million people worldwide. The risk of developing AD is significantly influenced by genetic factors. Deciphering their molecular functions has substantially advanced our understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms underlying AD. The PICALM gene represents a highly validated AD risk factor, and the encoded endocytic adaptor CALM is critical for endothelial A{beta} clearance and microglial A{beta} phagocytosis. However, it remains controversial how neuronally expressed CALM modulates AD pathogenesis. We find that loss of neuronal CALM accelerates A{beta} plaque formation and impairs neurotransmission in an AD mouse model, revealing a protective role for neuronal CALM. These phenotypes are accompanied by an elevated surface level of the endolysosomal SNARE protein VAMP8, consistent with a role for CALM in promoting the turnover of aggregated proteins via the autophagy/lysosome pathway. Moreover, loss of CALM promotes A{beta} aggregation in a C. elegans model expressing fluorescently labelled A{beta}, while neuron-specific overexpression of CALM decreases A{beta} aggregation. Finally, we demonstrate that the ANTH domain of CALM displays chaperone-like activity by inhibiting A{beta} aggregation in vitro. Our combined data suggest that neuronal CALM might counteract AD progression by suppressing A{beta} aggregation and by safeguarding endolysosomal SNARE trafficking.

metadata.title: PICALM deficiency exacerbates amyloid pathology in murine and nematode Alzheimers disease models

summary: Neuronal CALM loss accelerates amyloid plaque formation and impairs neurotransmission in mice; CALM also suppresses Aβ aggregation in C. elegans and in vitro.
